newsitem.title: INDIA: India air collision victims wait to be claimed.
newsitem.headline: India air collision victims wait to be claimed.

text.p: Scores of unidentified corpses from the world's worst mid-air disaster were bundled out of trucks into morgues at New Delhi hospitals on Friday, where they will wait until relatives identify them, officials said.

Indian authorities said 80 bodies, swaddled in burnt or ragged clothes, arrived in trucks packed with bloodstained ice slabs from the northern town of Charkhi Dadri, 80 kms (50 miles) west of New Delhi.
"If no one claims the bodies we will see to it that they are given proper respect and disposed of in an honourable manner," an official of the Airports Authority of India told Reuters.
But relatives complained bitterly over the way in which morgue workers threw bodies off the trucks onto stretchers on the floor.
"In my village we even treat animals better than how they are treating my sons," said Muhammad Rafeeq, from the eastern state of Bihar, as he watched helplessly.
Rafeeq's sons, Rehman and Zafar, were just two of the 349 people who died in the mid-air collision between a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 on Tuesday.
He had been unable to identify his sons' bodies. They were aboard the Saudi jet, on their way to jobs in the Gulf.

The trucks brought 48 bodies to New Delhi's All-India Institute of Medical Sciences hospital from Charkhi Dadri, where the two aeroplanes had crashed to earth in "flaming fireballs", according to eyewitnesses.
Another 32 were taken to the Lady Hardinge Hospital nearby.
Hospital officials bargained with ice vendors for fresh supplies of ice, to preserve the bodies as long as possible.
More than a dozen coffins waited nearby to take the bodies on their last journey.
There were no wails, or cries. There were just a few pairs of swollen eyes and barely audible sighs as relatives looked from one open skull to the next, from one torso to the next.
Shakeel, whose cousin Irfan had died, said he had glimpsed a torso with a beard similar to his cousin's. "The authorities told me it was Irfan," he said, speaking in Hindi.
But Noor Hasan, from Moradabad in Bihar, who was also looking for his brother's body, said it had a similar beard.
Police said 298 bodies had been recovered but only 124 identified. About 50 were sent to Delhi on Thursday and 80 followed on Friday in trucks lined with ice.

Searchers have faced huge difficulties in locating the remains of all the passengers, most of them Indians going to jobs in Saudi Arabia. Scores of the remains were too badly charred or mangled to be identified.
